item.title: {{run}}-mirror-1 synthetic announcement
item.description: {{run}}-article-body The whole synthetic article one, as the mirror carries it. Every sentence of this article was invented for the ai-news local test environment and describes nothing that exists. The fictional Lantern Ridge orchard cooperative keeps a small weather station on each of its eleven terraces, and for three seasons its members wrote the readings by hand into a shared ledger kept in the packing shed. The ledger worked while the cooperative was small. As the terraces grew, its pages filled with crossed out numbers, late entries and readings that nobody could match to a terrace, and the frost warnings it was meant to support arrived a day after the frost. This synthetic announcement describes how the imaginary cooperative replaced the ledger with a plain notebook program that runs on one shared computer in the shed. The program asks for three numbers at a time, the terrace, the temperature at dawn and the soil moisture at noon, and it refuses a reading that does not name a terrace. It keeps every reading it accepts in a single file, one line per reading, so that any member can open the file in a text editor and read it without the program. In the first fictional month the members entered four hundred and twelve readings, and the program refused nineteen of them, most because the terrace number was missing or belonged to a terrace that had been merged with its neighbour the year before. The cooperative did not try to make the program clever. It draws no charts and sends no messages. Instead, at the end of each day it prints a short page that lists the coldest terrace, the driest terrace and any terrace with no reading at all, and the page is pinned to the door of the shed where the morning crew gathers. The imaginary orchard manager, who is named in no record outside this fixture, says that the empty terrace line turned out to be the most useful part of the page, because a missing reading usually meant a broken station rather than a careless member. Over the fictional season the cooperative found and repaired four stations that had stopped working without anyone noticing. The article goes on to describe the limits of the approach. A single shared computer is a single point of failure, and on two invented mornings a power cut in the shed meant that nobody could enter readings until noon. The members now keep a paper card beside the computer for those mornings and type the card in when the power returns, which brings back a little of the old ledger, but only for a few hours at a time. The cooperative also learned that a reading entered late is still worth keeping, so the program now records both the time of the reading and the time it was typed, and the daily page marks any reading typed more than six hours after it was taken. Looking ahead, the fictional members plan to add a second shared computer in the upper barn and to compare the two files once a week by hand. They have decided against any automatic merge until they understand how often the two files disagree. This closing paragraph exists only so that the fixture carries a whole article of several thousand characters, the shape the mirror gives each item, and so that a test can check that none of this text is ever stored or shown by the app. The article ends here.

item.title: {{run}}-mirror-2 synthetic announcement
item.description: {{run}}-article-body The whole synthetic article two, as the mirror carries it. Like the first article of this fixture, it was invented for the ai-news local test environment, and no person, place or service in it exists. The imaginary Saltmarsh Point ferry service runs two small boats across a tidal channel, and its timetable has always been written on a chalkboard at each landing. Because the channel is shallow, a crossing that takes nine minutes at high water can take twenty five minutes at low water, when the boats must follow the long buoyed path around the sandbar. For years the fictional crews simply wrote the next three departures on the board each morning, guessing at the tide from experience, and passengers learned to arrive early and wait. This synthetic article tells how the service began to publish a printed weekly timetable instead. The crews started by keeping a simple log of every crossing for one invented month, with the departure time, the arrival time, the boat and a note on the water. From that log they worked out four crossing lengths, one for each quarter of the tidal range, and a rule for which length applied at each hour. The rule was written on a single sheet so that any crew member could apply it by hand without a calculator. The first printed timetable went up at both landings at the start of an imaginary spring. It listed every departure for the week, each marked with a small letter that showed which crossing length the crews expected. Passengers in the story responded to the letters more than to the times, because a letter told them whether to expect the short crossing or the long one around the bar. The service kept the chalkboards and now uses them only for changes on the day, such as a boat out of service or a crossing cancelled for fog. The article is candid about what went wrong. In the second fictional week a spring tide ran lower than any tide in the logged month, and the long path around the sandbar took thirty one minutes rather than twenty five, so every afternoon departure ran late. The crews responded by adding a fifth crossing length for the lowest tides and by logging every crossing again for a further month to check the rule. They also decided that the printed timetable would always state, in one plain sentence at the top, that times at the lowest tides are estimates. Looking ahead, the imaginary service intends to print the timetable a fortnight at a time rather than a week, once a second month of logs confirms the five crossing lengths. It has no plans for a screen at either landing, because the crews prefer a sheet that keeps working when the power at the landing fails. The crews also plan to keep the crossing log going for good, since a single unusual month taught them more about the channel than the many years of guessing that came before it. This closing paragraph exists only so that the fixture carries a whole article of several thousand characters, the shape the mirror gives each item, and so that a test can check that none of this text is ever stored or shown by the app. The second article ends here.
